name: Emeka Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Emeka. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work out of the Southgate depot, and these days most of our work is the new housing estates going up on the edge of the city. We run the feeder lines in, set the transformers, connect street after street of new houses. I usually drive and operate the bucket truck, so I'm the one up top making the connections while the ground crew feeds me materials. I like seeing a field turn into a neighbourhood with the lights on. What wears me out is the developers changing plans every week, so you turn up and the road you were meant to wire hasn't been built.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about home, and how you see your work fitting in.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Ana works in the office at Maya's primary school, and our son Tobi is thirteen. We bought a four-bedroom on one of the estates I actually wired, which I still find funny. The mortgage rate is fixed until next autumn, and then it renews, which I'm already thinking about. We've got about three months of money saved. I use AI now and then, mostly to check a building regulation or write a polite email to a developer who's messed us around. In my spare time I build furniture in the garage, tables and shelves, nothing fancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, there you go, it was useful for a few things and that's it. Like the satnav, handy, didn't change the world. I wouldn't make a big deal of it online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, honestly, it's good news. The houses still need wiring and the developers still need us. The only thing I'd worry about is the mortgage renewal, and that's about interest rates, not AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing the job, keep using the AI for emails and regs when it saves time. Put a bit more aside before the mortgage renews next autumn, maybe another hundred a month. That's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Business as usual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the mortgage renewal. What are you bracing for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our fixed rate ends next October. If rates stay where they are, the payment goes up maybe two hundred a month. So whatever happens with AI, that's the thing I'm planning round right now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of your job you'd hoped AI might help with?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The planning chaos with the developers. If something could keep the site drawings up to date and tell us which roads are actually ready, we'd waste half as many trips. But in this picture I guess we're still ringing the site manager.

S0.say: It was useful for a few things, like the satnav, and that's it. He wouldn't make a big deal of it online.
S0.think: It's good news for him, since the new houses still need wiring. His real worry is the mortgage renewal next autumn, which is about interest rates, not AI.
S0.do: Keeps working at the Southgate depot and uses AI for emails and building regulations when it helps. Saves about a hundred extra a month ahead of the mortgage renewal next October.
S0.quote: Like the satnav, handy, didn't change the world.
S0.fieldNote: Emeka is practical and plans around the concrete risks in front of him, like his mortgage rate. He uses AI as a handy tool without excitement or fear. He'd welcome help with the developer planning chaos.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's like any change, you adapt or you get left behind, but companies should help people through it. I'd want the company to be straight with us about what's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the new estates keep me busy for a while, but the planning side gets automated and maybe some inspection work goes to drones. I'm average at this job, not the best, so if they cut crews, I'm not first to be kept. That's the honest truth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the new tools once the first crews had tried them and the bugs were out. I'd look at getting my electrician's licence through evening classes, so I could do home solar and battery installs on the side, which is growing on these estates anyway. That's about a year and a half part-time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not losing sleep, but thinking about it on the drive home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why solar and batteries, specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because every new house I wire now has panels on the roof, and half the owners ask me who can fit a home battery. I already know the grid side. If I had the licence, I could do installs on Saturdays, and that's money that's mine, not the company's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Ana say about you doing evening classes on top of the job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say fine, as long as I'm still home for Maya's bedtime twice a week. And she'd ask me to stop buying wood for the furniture until the course is paid off. Fair enough.

S1.say: It's like any change: you adapt or get left behind, but companies should help people through it. He'd want the company to be straight about what's coming.
S1.think: The new estates keep him busy for a while, but planning and inspection get automated. As an average lineworker, he knows he wouldn't be first to be kept if crews were cut.
S1.do: Takes up new tools once the first crews have ironed out the bugs. Starts evening classes for an electrician's licence, about eighteen months part-time, to do home solar and battery installs on Saturdays.
S1.feel: Uneasy, thinking about it on the drive home but not losing sleep.
S1.quote: If I had the licence, I could do installs on Saturdays, and that's money that's mine, not the company's.
S1.fieldNote: His plan is grounded in what he sees on the job every day: rooftop panels and home batteries. He waits for others to test new tools before adopting them. His wife sets clear family limits on the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody's ready for this, so the government and the companies need to sit down now and work out a plan. Not panic, a plan. Some kind of income support, and slowing it down where it's not safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be scared. Two years, robots can do the wiring and the installs? Then the solar side business is gone too. And it lands right after our mortgage renews at a higher rate. Three months of savings looks very small then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away, I'd stop the furniture spending, cancel the summer trip and save every extra pound I could. I'd ask the bank about a longer mortgage term at renewal, to bring the payment down. And I'd look for whatever job is still around, maybe on the robot maintenance side, though everyone would be chasing that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd feel like I was driving at night with no headlights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still do the electrician course with only two years' warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not. By the time I finished, the robots would be doing it. I'd put that money in savings instead. That hurts a bit, it felt like a good plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Tobi?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tobi's thirteen and he's into computers, so he'd probably know more about it than me. I'd tell him we might have to tighten things for a while, and that it's not forever. I'd try to sound more sure than I was.

S2.say: Nobody's ready, so government and companies need to sit down now and work out a plan, not panic: income support and slowing it down where it isn't safe.
S2.think: He'd be scared, because robots doing wiring and installs would kill his side-business plan too. It would land just after the mortgage renews at a higher rate, with three months of savings.
S2.do: Stops furniture spending, cancels the summer trip and saves every extra bit. Asks the bank for a longer mortgage term at renewal and drops the electrician course, looking for any remaining job, possibly in robot maintenance.
S2.feel: Alarmed, like driving at night with no headlights.
S2.quote: By the time I finished, the robots would be doing it. I'd put that money in savings instead.
S2.fieldNote: The two-year timeline undoes his careful plan, and he felt the loss. The timing with his mortgage renewal sharpened his fear. He would try to sound more certain than he felt in front of his son.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short but workable, if people start now. I'd tell younger guys at the depot to think about what's next while they're still getting paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years gives me enough to finish the licence and maybe make some money from installs before the robots arrive. It doesn't save the job in the end, but it builds the cushion. Tobi would be eighteen, Maya fourteen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the electrician course next year and finish it by 2028. Do installs at weekends for two or three years and put that money toward the mortgage and savings, aiming for six months. Keep using the AI tools at work as they come in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but busy. Being busy helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the robots arrive in 2031, isn't the install work gone then too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, in the end. But two or three years of Saturday money, maybe a few hundred a month, is real money. It'd pay down the mortgage before I lose the main job. I see it as filling the tank before a long drive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of the five years would you dread most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the last year, 2030, when you can see the robots being trialled on other crews and you're waiting for your turn. I'd rather it were quick, in a way. But I'd also rather have the money.

S3.say: Five years is short but workable if people start now. He'd tell younger colleagues to plan their next step while still being paid.
S3.think: Five years is enough to finish the licence and earn from installs before the robots arrive. It won't save the job, but it builds the cushion.
S3.do: Starts the electrician course next year, finishing by 2028, then does weekend installs for two or three years. Puts that money toward the mortgage and savings, aiming for six months, while using new tools at work.
S3.feel: Anxious, but steadied by being busy.
S3.quote: I see it as filling the tank before a long drive.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, he treats his side-business plan as a way to build a cushion rather than a new career. He dreads the waiting near the end. His pragmatism shows in weighing a quick shock against more money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to get it right, so let's not mess it up. Sensible planning from the government, training money, and companies being honest about their timelines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels alright for me. I'd be 53. The kids would be grown, the mortgage much smaller. I'd do the licence, build the solar side, and maybe end up running a small business that manages the robots doing installs, or just retire a bit early if the money's there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Licence over the next two years, then build the install work slowly. Maybe invest a bit in my own tools and a van around year four if it's going well. Keep the day job as long as it lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more curious than worried. It's far enough away that I can think straight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Running a business that manages robots. What does that look like to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't know. Maybe I own two robots and a van and I'm the one customers call. Or maybe big companies do all of it and there's no room for a guy like me. I'd keep an eye on it and decide around 2032.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change anything for Tobi and Maya?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably spend more of the savings on their education than we'd planned, if that's what gives them a chance. Tobi wants to study computing. Maya wants to be a vet, or a pop star, depending on the day.

S4.say: Ten years is enough to get it right, so let's not mess it up: sensible government planning, training money and honest company timelines.
S4.think: Ten years feels alright: at 53 with grown kids and a smaller mortgage, he could build a solar install business or retire a bit early if the money is there.
S4.do: Gets the electrician's licence over two years and builds install work slowly. Invests in his own tools and a van around year four if it's going well, keeping the day job as long as it lasts.
S4.feel: Uneasy but more curious than worried, able to think straight.
S4.quote: Maybe I own two robots and a van and I'm the one customers call.
S4.fieldNote: The long runway lets his steady, step-by-step style work in his favour. He's honest that he doesn't know if there will be room for small operators. He'd shift savings toward his children's education.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, mostly because of the timing with the mortgage. What would help is the bank and the government making it easy to stretch or pause mortgage payments for people who lose work to robots, and some income support for a couple of years. Something to stop people losing their houses.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what we'd miss. I'd miss the moment when a new street lights up for the first time. You stand there at dusk and someone's turned on their kitchen light, and you did that. A robot won't care about that bit.

headlineQuote: You stand there at dusk and someone's turned on their kitchen light, and you did that.
portrait: Emeka Torres is a 43-year-old bucket-truck lineworker who wires new housing estates on the edge of the city, and lives with his wife Ana and two kids on an estate he wired himself. He is practical and numbers-minded, with three months of savings and a fixed mortgage rate that ends next autumn. He uses AI now and then and plans to get an electrician's licence for weekend solar and battery installs. Fast AGI alarms him because it would kill that plan just as his mortgage renews, while five or ten years let him use the side work to build a cushion and maybe a small business.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because it would hit just after his mortgage renews at a higher rate.
whatWouldHelp: Easy ways to stretch or pause mortgage payments for people who lose work to robots, plus a couple of years of income support so families keep their homes.
